item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
Collapsed for ease of scrolling.

+ show block
– hide block

I’d say the agent would be questioning the way The Foundation contains humanoid anomalies and the way it treats d-class.

My tentative recommendation would be to throw together a specific incident of some kind. That way, the holder's "confession" can be more emotional than a monologue about ethics and practices. Bonus points if you can tie it into the theme of subjective good and evil.

Personal destinies are things that people are always meant to do. They may not know on the beforehand, but they always feel very satisfied when they’re done.

If we disregard terminology, is this still destiny at all? Was the 'holder' destined to overthrow the site administrator? Were those small GOIs fated to crumble due to a single silly locket? Or is it just what happens as a consequence of an anomaly? In other words, how large-scale do the effects of personal destinies get before they stop being personal?

item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
I’d say the agent would be questioning the way The Foundation contains humanoid anomalies and the way it treats d-class. Both of which are fairly low clearance but also can be moral grey areas.

As for destiny, I’ll admit I’ve had a fairly flimsy definition. The idea of the locket is that it unlocks people’s personal destinies. There’s also the overarching force of destiny that forces people to touch it. Personal destinies are things that people are always meant to do. They may not know on the beforehand, but they always feel very satisfied when they’re done.

item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
I do like the change to make the locket somewhat utile to the Foundation. I would, however, like some clarification regarding this part:

After being interviewed the holder confesses that they’d been questioning the morality of the Foundation for some time but had never thought of doing anything about it.

What about the Foundation's practices would be called into question here? I know that might seem like a silly question, but every author tends to have different 'headcanons' regarding what the Foundation makes public knowledge among its staff. Would this be in regards to the containment procedures of specific anomalies, or the overarching philosophy of "Contain First, Ask Questions Later"?

As a side point, does this mean that the locket is no longer connected to 'destiny' as a supreme force? That might change things as well.

item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
MAJOR CHANGES

Well then, I know it’s been a while but I think I know what to do.

Earlier I said that the Foundation couldn’t aim this artifact. I’m changing that, they did weaponize it, for a time. The main thing I’m changing is the way it targets a villain. Instead of the locket having its own sense of right and wrong it targets someone the holder views as evil. The thing is, it targets anyone nearby that is evil enough, that’s always been how it works I’m just making it clear.

What I’m planning on adding is a program where the Foundation uses the locket to defeat some small GOIs. It works, for a time. Then during one attempt, the holder of the locket turns around and proceeds to attack the Foundation. Causing serious damage and even unseating a site administrator. After being interviewed the holder confesses that they’d been questioning the morality of the Foundation for some time but had never thought of doing anything about it. That’s when the Foundation realizes that no amount of psychology or loyalty tests can tell if someone truly, in their heart of hearts, believes the Foundation is good. So they discontinue the program.

Alright, here’s my take.

First off, I do like the unique take on containment this concept focuses on. If the Foundation is anything, it’s creative and cautious. Your idea seems to meet both of those, though I’m a bit iffy on the logic vis a vis why the task force needs to be kept in the dark.

Honestly, at this point, my main concern is that there’s missed opportunity here. The SCP universe isn’t exactly a canon with a lot of conventional moral dichotomies and heroes. Introducing an artifact that can both railroad Foundation attempts to suppress it and bring the ethical choices of the organization into question is a big idea that feels rather wasted on containment squabbles

item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded: Thanks for the critique! About what defines evil. It’s not about what is actually evil. In fact, I’m not planning on using the words “evil” or “villain” anywhere in the article. It’s just that there are some consistent traits across all people and organizations that the locket defeats. The Foundation has noticed that they meet these traits. You seem to be suggesting switching the focus to moral questioning. It’s a neat idea, I just don’t know where I’d go with it. Right now I’m mostly focusing on the containment of this. While an overhaul’s fine if necessary I’m not really sure what I’d write about with that idea. I’ll think about it though. Thanks again, it’s always good to hear another perspective after thinking about an idea for a while.

item.title: Re: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
(Can't give greenlights)

While interesting, the idea that the locket causes a person to be destined to defeat some objective evil is a bit too simplistic. Especially considering that evil is most often a matter of perspective. From the Foundation's point of view, their actions are completely justified, and other GoIs or SCPs are considered 'evil'.

+ Some more Critique
- Less Critique

Which is especially difficult due to catch two, the Foundation meets all the requirements to be a villain. So their top priority is obviously making sure they never get selected as a target.

How do the foundation know that they meet the requirements to be villains? Has the locket caused a person to go after another GoI or foundational personnel in the past? What are the requirements to be a villain? This sentiment would probably work better if the foundation was trying to keep the locket out of the hands of someone who considers the foundation evil.

For instance, what happens if you have someone touch the locket, then you terminate them? (Spoiler alert, the same thing that happens when the protagonist of a book is facing down a firing squad, it doesn’t end well for the firing squad).

The person affected by the locket is both incapable of dying and incapable of killing people.

This is an interesting and somewhat comedic idea, but it makes the locket somewhat generic and similar to other reality altering/ fate changing SCPs out there. Also, it brings up the question as to why the foundation doesn't use the locket's powers to dismantle other, more destructive, organizations. While the foundation isn't perfect, there are various cults and GoIs that cause more human suffering and chaos the they do.

Overall, an interesting idea. The foundation trying to fight fate is a fairly interesting idea, but the properties of the locket could use some refinement. This could be a great narrative to explore what constitutes 'evil', but just making it something that wants to take down the foundation is a bit boring.

item.title: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: An old locket, when someone touches it they begin on a journey to face some evil person or organization. They’ll defeat the villain in some epic showdown and everyone lives happily ever after.

+ Yay! Happily ever after!
- Yeah, of course there’s more

There’s a few catches. First, someone always touches the locket, it’s destiny. That’s not to say that this is uncontainable, but the journeys need to be managed instead of prevented. Which is especially difficult due to catch two, the Foundation meets all the requirements to be a villain. So their top priority is obviously making sure they never get selected as a target. But then comes in catch three, because the obvious containment method is to simply send someone on a scripted adventure. But when you script the adventure, you become the villain. I don’t know if you’ve caught on by now but this article is all about the Foundation trying to contain fate, which is completely illogical. But the thing is, they do it.

Central Narrative: The meat of the story will be told through test logs where the Foundation will experiment with different containment procedures. For instance, what happens if you have someone touch the locket, then you terminate them? (Spoiler alert, the same thing that happens when the protagonist of a book is facing down a firing squad, it doesn’t end well for the firing squad). In the end, they contain it by having an independent task force act as the villains. The task force doesn’t know they’re meant to be villains, they know that they have one objective, “kill anyone who touches the locket”. They also know that they keep failing. Since the task force isn’t directly controlled by the Foundation, the Foundation is safe from becoming the villains.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Two things. One, fate isn’t that common of a system to show up in SCPs. The second one I haven’t mentioned yet, but this is actually a completely non lethal SCP. The person affected by the locket is both incapable of dying and incapable of killing people. That’s not to say it’s not dangerous though. I’m considering adding a discovery log where someone with this locket collapses a corporation that was exploiting people, but at the same time puts millions of people out of work.

Additional Notes: I want to know if you think this is too many ideas in one or if it ties together well. MAJOR CHANGES BELOW
